entities.summary:
The Treaty of Ankara, signed on October 20, 1921, marked a pivotal moment in Turkish and French relations following the tumultuous aftermath of World War I. This agreement was forged between the Grand National Assembly of Turkey, led by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, and the French Republic, under Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau. By establishing a diplomatic framework, this treaty significantly impacted the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East and solidified Turkey's sovereignty in the wake of the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, highlighting the emergence of national self-determination in the post-war era.

The core events leading to the Treaty of Ankara were rooted in the broader context of the Turkish War of Independence (1919-1923), during which Turkish forces, seeking to rid their territory of foreign occupation, engaged in military confrontations against both Greek and French troops. The treaty outlined mutual recognition of territorial integrity and established boundaries, particularly addressing issues in the regions of Cilicia and the southeastern territories of Turkey, which had been the focus of French interests during the war. It was a culmination of negotiations that underscored the desire of both nations to stabilize their respective political situations, culminating in Turkey gaining recognition of its borders and enhanced diplomatic relations with France.
